items.headline: New: Japan's Nikkei closes down 2.4%, back below 60,000; Advantest sinks 11%
items.caption: Chip stocks dragged Tokyo lower ahead of Nvidia's results. Two names, Advantest and Tokyo Electron, caused most of the drop.

detail: Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.4%, or about 1,480 points, to 59,662. It was the index's first close below 60,000 in a week. The broader Topix fell only about 1%.
Two chip stocks did most of the damage. Advantest, which supplies Nvidia, fell 11.1%. Tokyo Electron fell 7.1%. Together they took about 1,072 points off the Nikkei.
Investors are nervous about turmoil at Nvidia before its earnings report later today. Anthropic's IPO is also set to price Wednesday and start trading Thursday.
money: A price-weighted index like the Nikkei can swing on a few big stocks; check what your Japan fund actually holds.
If you own chip suppliers, Nvidia's report tonight is a big catalyst; decide your plan before the news, not after.
The broader Topix fell much less, a reminder that wide index funds can soften single-sector shocks.

items.headline: 2027 retirement limits: 401(k) rises $1,000 to $25,500; IRA limit stays $7,500
items.caption: The IRS raised workplace plan limits for 2027. Savers 50 and older can put in up to $34,000; those 60 to 63 get a bigger catch-up.

visual.title: 2027 retirement contribution limits
visual.foot: Total for 50+ in most plans: $34,000

detail: The IRS set 2027 limits for retirement savings. Workers can put up to $25,500 into a 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 or Thrift Savings Plan, up $1,000 from 2026.
The catch-up for people 50 and older rises to $8,500, for a total of $34,000. People aged 60 to 63 get a larger catch-up of $11,750.
IRA limits did not change: $7,500, plus a $1,100 catch-up for those 50 and up. Income ranges for deductible IRAs, Roth IRAs and the Saver's Credit all went up.

items.headline: ICE detains two Argentine acrobats at Phoenix airport despite work permits to 2029
items.caption: The married performers have pending asylum cases and no criminal records. ICE says a pending application doesn't give legal status.
detail: ICE agents detained Agustín Baccega, 42, and Gustavo Romanello, 34, a married couple of Argentine acrobats, at Phoenix Sky Harbor Airport on November 7. They were flying in from Orlando for a fellow performer's funeral, Latin Times reported Monday.
Both held US work permits valid through 2029 and had pending asylum claims. ICE classified them as visa overstays from 2021. Neither has a criminal record or a prior deportation order.

An ICE spokesperson said work authorization or a pending application does not grant legal status. Their lawyer criticized the arrests. The airport says it gets no advance notice and does not share passenger data with ICE.
money: Immigrants with pending cases may want to talk with a lawyer before domestic travel.
Families facing detention often face sudden legal and bail costs; nonprofit legal aid can lower them.

risk: Each case depends on individual facts and court outcomes.

items.headline: HUD rule: every household member must prove eligible status; 90 days to document
items.caption: The rule takes effect Dec. 14. HUD estimates about 24,000 ineligible residents; advocates say about 80,000 people in mixed-status homes could be affected.
detail: HUD published a final rule requiring every member of an assisted household to show US citizenship or eligible immigration status. It takes effect Dec. 14, and households get 90 days to submit documents. Checks run through DHS's SAVE system.

Prorated aid for mixed-status households becomes temporary during verification. HUD estimates about 24,000 ineligible residents in roughly 20,000 households and frames the rule as protecting taxpayers.

items.headline: US moves to stop China from renting AI chips abroad; new licenses for five countries
items.caption: A new Commerce rule targets remote access to advanced AI chips in third-country data centers. Shipping them to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil now needs extra licenses.

visual.title: The remote-access chip rule
items: Targets renting chip power in third-country data centers
Extra licenses for Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand
Follows Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia last week

detail: The Commerce Department issued an interim rule on Monday that limits remote access to advanced AI chips. It aims to stop restricted buyers, such as Chinese firms, from renting computing power in data centers outside China.
The rule adds license requirements to export, re-export or transfer advanced chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. It treats remote access more like physical shipments.
It comes days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO and ahead of Trump's meeting with China's Xi this week.
money: Chip and cloud stocks with big Southeast Asia sales could see guidance changes; listen for comments on Nvidia's call Tuesday.
If you own a broad chip fund, rules like this hit many names at once; diversification beyond one sector helps.
Volatility around policy news can create entry points for long-term buyers, but go in slowly.

Buying talent is a common AI strategy; watch whether the deal shows up in new products before paying up for the story.

items.headline: Fed's Barr: AI agents moving money on their own could turn bank runs into minutes
items.caption: Fed Governor Michael Barr warned that many AI agents reacting to the same signal could pull deposits at once. He urged strict consent and limits on what agents can do.

visual.title: How fast runs can be
visual.label: Silicon Valley Bank lost about $42 billion in one day in March 2023, with humans clicking.

detail: Speaking in Milan on Monday, Fed Governor Michael Barr said autonomous AI agents could speed up bank runs by moving deposits automatically when they spot yield gaps or stress.

His biggest worry is herd behavior: many agents built on similar models could react to the same signal in seconds. He also said bad actors could feed false information to many systems at once, and that banks already see agents trying actions in accounts without verified consent.
Barr suggested strict authentication, consent tied to each action, and technical limits on agents. He did not propose a new rule.
money: Keep deposits under the $250,000 FDIC limit per bank, per ownership category, so a run doesn't put your cash at risk.
Before giving any AI tool access to your bank account, check what it can do without asking you.
Turn on account alerts so you see any money movement right away.
risk: Rules for AI agents in banking are still unsettled.
Scammers may pose as AI assistants to get account access.

sources.t: Fed's Barr warns AI agents could turn bank runs into minutes-long events

items.headline: Supreme Court ends crypto bank Custodia's fight for a Fed master account
items.caption: The justices declined to hear the case, leaving a ruling that Fed banks can reject even eligible applicants. It's a setback for crypto banks seeking direct Fed access.
detail: The Supreme Court on Monday denied Custodia Bank's petition, leaving in place a Tenth Circuit ruling that Federal Reserve banks have discretion to reject master account applications, even from legally eligible banks.
Custodia, a Wyoming-chartered crypto bank, applied in October 2020 and was denied in January 2023. Lower courts sided with the Fed in 2024 and 2025.
A master account lets a bank plug straight into the Fed's payment system. Kraken got a limited master account in March 2026.
money: If you hold cash at a crypto firm, check whether it's FDIC-insured through a partner bank; most crypto balances are not.
Crypto banks without Fed access rely on other banks, which can mean higher fees or slower transfers.
Keep emergency cash at a regular insured bank or credit union.
risk: Crypto banks may face more limits on payment access.

detail: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro wants to raise the state minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 an hour, about a 107% jump. He says it will be the first bill he signs in January 2027, after Democrats flipped the state Senate.
About half a million Pennsylvania workers earn less than $15. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is pushing Congress to raise the federal $7.25 rate.

Some economists warn steep raises can lead to price hikes, fewer hours or slower hiring, especially for entry-level workers. Other research has found little job loss in restaurants after past increases.

items.headline: ICE made nearly 18,000 arrests in New Jersey since 2025; fewer had convictions
items.caption: ICE data shows arrests in 324 New Jersey towns from January 2025 to July 2026. The share with criminal convictions fell from 36% to 13%.

visual.title: ICE arrests in New Jersey
visual.label: Arrests from January 2025 through July 2026, per ICE records.

detail: ICE made nearly 18,000 arrests across 324 New Jersey municipalities between January 2025 and July 2026, according to federal records obtained by the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by NorthJersey.com.
There were 9,103 arrests in 2025 and about 8,700 in the first seven months of 2026. Newark led with nearly 4,400, followed by Elizabeth and Mount Laurel.
The share of people arrested with criminal convictions fell from 36% in January 2025 to 13% in July 2026. Nationally, ICE made over half a million arrests in the same period.
money: Employers in heavy-arrest areas may face worker shortages; plan staffing and keep I-9 records in order.
Families can keep key documents and contacts organized and find a licensed immigration attorney in advance.

items.headline: California's next insurance chief pitches state-run disaster coverage for homeowners
items.caption: Commissioner-elect Jane Kim wants a public catastrophe insurance plan beyond the FAIR Plan. Republicans worry taxpayers would carry the risk.

visual.title: Home insurance in California
visual.label: What homeowners pay each year to insure their homes.

detail: Jane Kim, a former San Francisco supervisor elected California insurance commissioner, proposes a single-payer natural disaster insurance plan for homeowners that goes beyond the state's FAIR Plan.

Under her idea, the state would replace private insurers on catastrophe claims, invest premiums, and send extra profits into fire and flood prevention. She says it is modeled on Spain, France and New Zealand and would cost taxpayers nothing.

Homeowners pay about $18 billion a year for coverage, with $3 billion to $6 billion going to wildfire risk. Republican leader Roger Niello called a taxpayer guarantee too risky. Kim takes office Jan. 4.
money: Shop your homeowners policy now; prices and options may shift as the new commissioner sets policy.
Home-hardening steps like vents and defensible space can lower premiums with some insurers.
If you're on the FAIR Plan, look at a 'difference in conditions' policy to fill coverage gaps.
risk: The plan needs lawmakers' approval and could change a lot.
A state-backed fund could face big losses after a major disaster.
